mission.title: Evidence, Claims and the Limits of Generalisation

theory.title: Evidence, claims and the limits of generalisation
theory.explanation: A result can be accurately measured and still be overinterpreted. Ask who was studied, how participants were selected, which groups were absent and whether the sample resembles the population to which the claim is applied. Sampling bias, self-selection, confounding variables and narrow settings can restrict external validity. Replication strengthens confidence in a finding, but it does not automatically make an unrepresentative sample representative. Distinguish statistical significance from practical importance, association from causation, and a result observed in one context from a claim about a wider population. At C2 level, state precisely what the evidence supports, identify what remains uncertain and specify what further evidence would change the conclusion.
theory.tip: Trace the chain from population → sampling frame → sample → measurement → finding → generalisation. At each step, ask who or what may have been excluded and whether an alternative explanation remains plausible.

patterns.label: Scope of inference
patterns.pattern: Limit a claim to the population and conditions actually studied.
examples: The findings may apply to the participating clinics, but cannot yet be extrapolated to the national population.

patterns.label: Sampling limitations
patterns.pattern: Identify selection effects and missing perspectives.
examples: Because participation was voluntary, respondents may have been more engaged than non-participants.

patterns.label: Corroboration and replication
patterns.pattern: Separate independent confirmation from repetition within the same dataset.
examples: The pattern has been replicated in a second setting, although both studies used similar recruitment methods.

patterns.label: Proportionate conclusion
patterns.pattern: Match the strength of the wording to the strength and reach of the evidence.
examples: The results are consistent with the hypothesis, but further research is needed before a broader claim can be made.

content.passage:
A regional health authority announced that a pilot programme had reduced missed appointments by 18 per cent. The headline was compelling, and the report recommended extending the intervention nationally. Yet the evaluation had taken place in four clinics that had volunteered to participate. Their staff had received additional training, and patients had been contacted through a messaging system not available in every region.

The figures themselves were not disputed. The difficulty lay in the leap from an observed change in those clinics to a claim about the programme's likely effect elsewhere. Clinics that volunteered may have had more committed managers; their patient populations may also have differed from those served by less well-resourced practices. These factors could have influenced the outcome independently of the intervention. Without a comparison capable of addressing such differences, the causal interpretation remained provisional.

Nor would a larger sample necessarily settle the matter if recruitment continued to favour clinics with similar characteristics. Representativeness concerns how cases enter a study, not merely how many cases it contains. Independent replication in settings with different staffing levels, patient profiles and communication systems would provide a stronger test of external validity.

A defensible conclusion would therefore be narrower: the pilot was associated with fewer missed appointments in the participating clinics and merits further evaluation under varied conditions. Such wording does not diminish the result. It distinguishes what was observed from what is being inferred, preserving the practical value of the evidence without overstating its reach.

content.audioTranscript: The evaluation team welcomed the reduction in missed appointments but cautioned against extending the conclusion too far. The clinics had volunteered, and their staffing levels were unusually high. One analyst noted that the sample was therefore unlikely to represent every practice in the region. Another said that the pattern was encouraging, although the study could not rule out other explanations. The team recommended independent replication in a more diverse group of settings before the authority made a national claim.
